h: تماشے کے پیچھے کی خبر: بلی ماران سے لکھنؤ تک بگڑی لسٹیں
dek: کلپنا شرما کے مطابق بیریکیڈ پھلانگتے لیڈروں کی تصویروں کے شور میں وہ زمینی ثبوت دب رہے ہیں جو بتاتے ہیں کہ ووٹر لسٹوں میں گڑبڑی کتنی گہری ہے۔
body: میڈیا پر اپنے کالم میں کلپنا شرما مانتی ہیں کہ ووٹر لسٹوں کی خصوصی گہری نظر ثانی (SIR) کا جھگڑا ٹھنڈا پڑنے والا نہیں، پر ٹی وی اور اخبار جس حصے پر کیمرہ ٹکائے ہوئے ہیں، وہ ہے راہل گاندھی کا بیریکیڈ پر چڑھنا، پرینکا گاندھی کا آئین لے کر سڑک پر لیٹنا اور کاکروچ جنتا پارٹی کے نوجوانوں کی سوشل میڈیا والی نمائش۔ مصنفہ کے مطابق یہ سب تماشا ہے، خبر کہیں اور ہے۔

پہلی مثال دہلی کی ہے۔ رپورٹرز کلیکٹو کی چھان بین بتاتی ہے کہ چھوٹے ووٹروں کے گھر جانے کے کمیشن کے حکم کا مطلب ہے کہ ہر بوتھ افسر کو دو مہینے میں اوسطاً 215 گھروں تک پہنچنا ہوگا، جبکہ بوتھ افسروں کی اپنی نوکریاں ہیں، کئی تو اسکول میں پڑھاتے ہیں۔ 661 بوتھوں پر 30 سے 70 فیصد ووٹر 'مشکوک' ٹھہرا دیے گئے۔ پرانی دہلی کے بلی ماران میں درج 635 میں سے 609 ووٹر اس ٹھپے کے نیچے آ گئے۔

بنگال میں سپریم کورٹ کے کہنے پر بنے ٹریبونل کام ہی نہیں کر پا رہے، کیونکہ کمیشن کے پورٹل سے نوٹس بھیجنے کا انتظام مہینوں بعد بھی نہیں بنا۔ اتر پردیش کا حساب اور الجھا ہوا ہے: فارم 6 کی 71.38 لاکھ درخواستیں آئیں، پر آخری لسٹ میں 84.3 لاکھ نام جڑ گئے، یعنی 12.92 لاکھ ناموں کی کوئی درخواست ہی نہیں دکھتی۔

ریجی نگر اور نندی گرام کے ضمنی انتخابات کی خبریں بھی اسی کڑی میں ہیں۔ الزام ہے کہ مسلم اکثریت والے ریجی نگر میں کئی مسلمانوں کو بوتھ سے لوٹا دیا گیا اور مقامی صحافیوں کے سوشل میڈیا پیج ووٹنگ ختم ہونے تک بند رکھے گئے، تاکہ کوئی زمینی ریکارڈ نہ بچے۔

شرما کہتی ہیں کہ ان رپورٹوں کو ساتھ رکھ کر پڑھیں تو تصویر صاف ہے: کٹے نام، ٹھپ پورٹل، بے حساب جڑے نام اور ضمنی انتخاب میں پولیس کا برتاؤ۔ کالم کے آخر میں وہ مہاراشٹر کے سوکھے کی طرف اشارہ کرتی ہیں، جہاں 358 میں سے 265 تعلقے سوکھے کی زد میں ہیں، یعنی وہ ملک جہاں کیمرہ آسانی سے نہیں جاتا۔
nazar: یہ کالم تحریک کی تنقید نہیں، اس کی یادداشت ہے۔ سڑک پر غصہ تبھی ٹکے گا جب ہر ریلی کے ساتھ بلی ماران جیسے بوتھوں کے اعداد و شمار بھی چلیں۔ جن محلوں میں زیادہ تر نام ایک جھٹکے میں شک کے گھیرے میں آ گئے، وہاں کے غریب، مسلمان اور مہاجر مزدور کسی کیمرے کے بھروسے نہیں، ثبوت کے بھروسے ہی اپنا ووٹ واپس پا سکتے ہیں۔
میڈیا کے لیے بھی سبق صاف ہے: بیریکیڈ کی تصویر ایک دن بکتی ہے، لسٹ کی چھان بین جمہوریت بچاتی ہے۔

h: اپوزیشن متحد، اب جواب دہی کی باری کمیشن کی
dek: دیش بندھو میں راجیش پانڈے کی دلیل: ووٹر لسٹ پر اٹھے سوالوں نے بکھری اپوزیشن کو ایک مشترکہ مسئلہ دے دیا ہے، پر ریلیوں سے آگے زمینی تنظیم کے بغیر بات ادھوری رہے گی۔
body: راجیش پانڈے اس مضمون میں دو باتوں کو ساتھ رکھ کر دیکھتے ہیں: اپوزیشن کا بڑھتا اتحاد اور انتخابی گڑبڑی کے الزاموں سے جمہوریت کو پیدا ہوا خطرہ۔ ان کے مطابق 1 نومبر کو رام لیلا میدان کی مشترکہ ریلی، عدالتوں میں دائر مقدمے اور طالب علموں، کارکنوں کی سرگرمی بتاتی ہے کہ الیکشن کمیشن کی ساکھ پر لوگوں کی بے چینی اب صرف پارٹیوں تک محدود نہیں رہی۔ گیانیش کمار خاموش ہیں اور بی جے پی بچاؤ میں ہے، پر خامیوں کا جواب نہیں آیا۔

مصنف کے مطابق ایس آئی آر کے ذریعے 13 کروڑ سے زیادہ نام لسٹوں سے ہٹے، اور خامیاں سامنے آنے پر کمیشن کو فارم 6 کی تبدیلیاں واپس لینی پڑیں اور ECINET کی جانچ کے لیے ماہرین کی کمیٹی بنانی پڑی۔ دو الیکشن کمشنروں نے لکھ کر اعتراض درج کیا کہ کچھ بڑے فیصلے ان کی جانکاری کے بغیر کمیشن کے نام پر لیے گئے، جبکہ کمیشن سپریم کورٹ میں کہتا ہے کہ فیصلے اتفاق رائے سے ہوئے۔

یوپی میں ووٹر اعداد و شمار کا میل نہ کھانا، پیلی بھیت میں دو الیکٹورل رجسٹریشن افسروں کی معطلی، کرناٹک میں 99.32 لاکھ ناموں کا کٹنا اور بغیر وجہ بھرے گئے قریب 61 ہزار فارم 7، یہ سب مصنف کی نظر میں ایسی گڑبڑیاں ہیں جن کے لیے اب تک کسی کی جواب دہی طے نہیں ہوئی۔ امت شاہ کے تین کروڑ دراندازوں والے دعوے پر وہ پوچھتے ہیں کہ اگر یہ سچ ہے تو انہیں ملک سے باہر کیوں نہیں بھیجا گیا۔

مضمون لوہیا کے دور، 1977 کی جنتا پارٹی اور 1989 کے جنتا دل کو یاد کرتا ہے، جو زیادہ تر کم دن چلے۔ مصنف کے مطابق اس بار فرق یہ ہے کہ مسئلہ انتخاب کی ایمانداری اور کمیشن کی جواب دہی کا ہے، جو سب کو جوڑنے والی زمین بن سکتا ہے۔

پر نتیجے میں چیتاونی بھی ہے: صرف ریلیاں کافی نہیں ہوں گی۔ خاص کر کانگریس، جسے مصنف تنظیم کے لحاظ سے کمزور مانتے ہیں، کو کارکنوں کو گاؤں محلے تک اتارنا ہوگا۔ ان کا بھروسا ہے کہ عوام کا دباؤ بنے تو ادارے جواب دیتے ہیں۔
nazar: مضمون کی طاقت اس کی فہرست ہے: فارم 6 سے لے کر فارم 7 اور پیلی بھیت تک، یہ دکھاتا ہے کہ الزام ہوا میں نہیں، ٹھوس انتظامی چوکوں پر ٹکے ہیں، حالانکہ 13 کروڑ جیسے اعداد مصنف کے اپنے ہیں اور ان کی آزاد جانچ ہونی چاہیے۔ کمزوری یہ ہے کہ راہل گاندھی کی قیادت کی تعریف کچھ زیادہ بھروسے سے کی گئی ہے، جبکہ ریاستوں میں سیٹوں کی کھینچ تان ابھی باقی ہے۔
سب سے کام کی بات آخری پیراگراف میں ہے۔ جنتر منتر اور رام لیلا میدان نے ماحول بنایا، پر جس کا نام کٹا ہے وہ بوتھ پر اکیلا کھڑا ہے۔ تحریک کا اگلا امتحان وہیں ہوگا۔

h: دو کمشنروں کے چودہ اعتراض: استعفیٰ کیوں ضروری ہے
dek: پی جان جے کینیڈی کے مطابق گیانیش کمار کے خلاف ثبوت باہر سے نہیں، کمیشن کے اندر سے آئے ہیں، اور اصل جڑ تقرری کا 2023 والا قانون ہے۔
body: کینیڈی دو سوالوں کو الگ کرتے ہیں: کیا کوئی گروپ دباؤ ڈال کر استعفیٰ لے سکتا ہے، اور کیا اس مانگ کے پیچھے ٹھوس بنیاد ہے۔ پہلے کا جواب دھرمیندر پردھان کے استعفے میں مل چکا ہے۔ دوسرے سوال کے لیے مصنف کمیشن کے اپنے کاغذوں کی طرف دیکھتے ہیں۔

انڈین ایکسپریس کی چھان بین کے حوالے سے وہ بتاتے ہیں کہ الیکشن کمشنر سکھبیر سنگھ سندھو اور وویک جوشی نے دس مہینوں میں کم سے کم چودہ بار لکھ کر اعتراض درج کیا، ایک دن میں چار بار بھی۔ قاعدہ کہتا ہے کہ فیصلے اتفاق سے ہوں یا اکثریت سے۔ مصنف کی دلیل ہے کہ جب تین میں سے دو ممبر لکھ کر اختلاف جتائیں اور پھر بھی فیصلہ لاگو ہو جائے، تو طریقہ کار ٹوٹ چکا ہے۔

تین مثالیں وہ گناتے ہیں۔ ووٹر ڈیٹا کے ڈیجیٹل نظام ECINet کو ایک جگہ مرکوز کرنے پر جوشی کا اعتراض، کیونکہ اس سے نام جوڑنے ہٹانے کا قانونی حق رکھنے والے ضلع افسروں کی طاقت گھٹتی ہے۔ گوا کے 97 ووٹر، جنہیں مقامی افسر نے اہل پایا، پر سافٹ ویئر نے یہ فیصلہ درج ہی نہیں ہونے دیا۔ اور فارم 6 میں ماں باپ یا دادا دادی کے پرانی لسٹ میں ہونے کا سوال، جس کے لیے قاعدوں میں کوئی ترمیم نہیں ہوئی۔ بنگال میں کمیشن کے نام سے داخل قریب 16 لاکھ اپیلوں کا ذمہ دار کون ہے، یہ بھی دونوں کمشنر طے نہیں کر پائے۔
مصنف کے مطابق جڑ 2023 کا قانون ہے، جس نے سلیکشن کمیٹی سے چیف جسٹس کو ہٹا کر وزیر اعظم کی پسند کا وزیر بٹھا دیا، یعنی سرکار کے پاس تین میں سے دو ووٹ۔ اسے بدلے بغیر چہرہ بدلنے سے کچھ نہیں ہوگا۔

پھر بھی وہ اپنی مرضی سے استعفے کی وکالت کرتے ہیں۔ ہٹانے کا آئینی طریقہ بہت مشکل ہے، اور زبردستی کی وداعی ہار جیسی دکھے گی، جبکہ استعفیٰ یہ پیغام دے گا کہ عہدہ اپنی ذمہ داری سمجھتا ہے۔ باقی گڑبڑیوں کے لیے الگ آڈٹ چاہیے۔
nazar: یہ مضمون تحریک کو ایک ضروری ڈسپلن دیتا ہے: نعرہ ایک آدمی کے خلاف ہو سکتا ہے، پر مانگ پورے ڈھانچے کی ہونی چاہیے۔ رام لیلا میدان سے بنگلورو تک پاس ہوئی قراردادوں میں تقرری قانون کی واپسی کی مانگ اسی سمجھ سے نکلتی ہے۔ گوا کے 97 ووٹروں کی کہانی بتاتی ہے کہ سافٹ ویئر جب افسر سے بڑا ہو جائے، تو نقصان سب سے پہلے اسی کا ہوتا ہے جس کے پاس شکایت کرنے کا کوئی راستہ نہیں۔

h: درانداز: ہر بار ناکام، پھر بھی وہی راگ
dek: دیش بندھو میں لوک لہر کے ایڈیٹر کی دلیل: ایس آئی آر نے کروڑوں نام کاٹے پر غیر ملکی گنتی کے ملے، اور رام لیلا میدان کے بعد بھی بی جے پی کے پاس 'درانداز' کے ڈر کے سوا کوئی جواب نہیں۔
body: مصنف 1 نومبر کی ریلی کو 'مودی شاہی' کے خاتمے کی شروعات مانتے ہیں، کیونکہ ان کی نظر میں ووٹ چوری کی مہم کا جواب دینے کے لیے سنگھ اور بی جے پی پھر اسی پرانے ہتھیار پر لوٹ آئے ہیں: یہ ڈر کہ درانداز ملک میں گھس ہی نہیں آئے، چھا بھی گئے ہیں۔ امت شاہ نے کہا کہ ایس آئی آر میں نام کٹنے کی شکایتیں دراصل دراندازوں کو بچانے کی کوشش ہیں۔

مضمون کے مطابق وزارت داخلہ بارہ سال سے زیادہ وقت سے پارلیمنٹ اور آر ٹی آئی کے جوابوں میں کہتی آئی ہے کہ دراندازوں کا اس کے پاس کوئی ٹھوس اعداد و شمار نہیں ہے۔ آسام کا این آر سی اس کی مثال ہے: بھاری خرچ اور غریبوں کی پریشانی کے بعد قریب 20 لاکھ لوگ مشکوک شہریت کے گھیرے میں آئے، اور جب پتہ چلا کہ ان میں دو تہائی ہندو ہیں، تو مصنف کے مطابق بی جے پی سرکار نے خود این آر سی کو ٹھکرا دیا۔

مصنف کہتے ہیں کہ ایس آئی آر نے یہی کہانی دہرائی۔ بہار میں قریب ایک کروڑ نام کٹے پر کمیشن نے نہیں بتایا کہ ان میں غیر ملکی کتنے تھے؛ مضمون کے مطابق چھ کروڑ سے زیادہ ووٹروں میں 600 سے کم غیر ملکی نکلے۔ میڈیا کی چھان بینوں کے حوالے سے وہ بتاتا ہے کہ چھ ریاستوں میں 9.96 کروڑ ووٹروں کی جانچ میں صرف 1600 غیر ملکی ملے، اور کرناٹک میں کٹے 99.7 لاکھ ناموں میں 716 غیر ملکی تھے، جن میں 545 نیپالی۔

سب سے دلچسپ بات اتر پردیش سے ہے۔ مضمون کے مطابق وزیر اعلیٰ یوگی آدتیہ ناتھ نے پارٹی کی میٹنگ میں کہا کہ ریاست میں 1.27 کروڑ ہندو ووٹ کٹے ہیں اور کارکنوں سے بی جے پی کے 'کمل ایپ' کے ذریعے انہیں جڑوانے کو کہا۔ مصنف کے لیے یہ ایس آئی آر کے اعلان شدہ مقصد کی پول ہے۔

نتیجہ یہ ہے کہ درانداز زیادہ تر پروپیگنڈے میں ہی بستے ہیں، جبکہ اصل قیمت غریب اور حاشیے کے ہندو، مسلمان اور عورتیں چکا رہی ہیں، جن کا ووٹ اور شہریت دونوں داؤ پر ہیں۔ بی جے پی صدر کا 'تین کروڑ درانداز' والا دعویٰ، مصنف کے مطابق، اسی ناکام ہتھیار کی واپسی ہے۔
nazar: مضمون کا سب سے اثردار حصہ اس کی گنتی ہے: کروڑوں نام کٹے، غیر ملکی ہزار دو ہزار۔ اگر یہ اعداد صحیح ہیں، اور مصنف انہیں میڈیا کی چھان بینوں سے لا رہے ہیں، تو ایس آئی آر کا اعلان شدہ مقصد اور اس کا نتیجہ ایک دوسرے سے میل نہیں کھاتے۔ یہ سوال کمیشن سے پوچھا جانا چاہیے، بی جے پی سے نہیں۔

'خاتمے کی شروعات' جیسی پیشین گوئی جوش میں لکھی گئی ہے، اسے ویسے ہی پڑھیں۔ پر این آر سی کا سبق اہم ہے: 'درانداز' کا ڈر جس پر سب سے پہلے گرتا ہے، وہ کاغذوں سے کمزور غریب ہے، چاہے اس کا مذہب کوئی بھی ہو۔

h: رشی آنند: یہ چوک نہیں، جمہوریہ کے خلاف سازش ہے
dek: اپنے سب اسٹیک پر رشی آنند کا الزام ہے کہ چیف الیکشن کمشنر نے عدالت اور عوام دونوں کو گمراہ کیا، اور اس کا حساب مواخذے سے آگے جانا چاہیے۔
body: رشی آنند کا مضمون کسی نرمی کے موڈ میں نہیں ہے۔ ان کی شروعات انڈین ایکسپریس کی اس رپورٹ سے ہے جس میں دو الیکشن کمشنروں کے چودہ تحریری اختلافات کی تفصیل تھی: فیصلوں سے اندھیرے میں رکھا جانا، میٹنگوں کا ایجنڈا اور کارروائی کا ریکارڈ نہ بننا، فارموں میں بغیر منظوری تبدیلی اور ووٹر ڈیٹا کو ایک جگہ مرکوز کرنا۔ مصنف کے مطابق کمیشن کی صفائی والی پریس ریلیز نے ان باتوں کو جھٹلانے کے بجائے پکا ہی کیا۔

ان کی نظر میں معاملہ اس سے بڑا ہے۔ جون 2025 میں بہار الیکشن سے کچھ مہینے پہلے SIR اچانک اعلان ہوا، پر کسی میٹنگ یا جائزے کا ریکارڈ نہیں ہے اور حق اطلاعات کی درخواستیں بھی لوٹا دی گئیں۔ ملک بھر میں مسودہ لسٹوں سے 13.37 کروڑ نام کٹے۔ مصنف کا اندازہ ہے کہ ہر سات میں سے ایک بالغ لسٹ سے باہر رہ سکتا ہے، اور ثابت کرنے کا بوجھ شہری پر ڈال کر ووٹ کو حق سے رعایت بنا دیا گیا۔

بنگال کے بارے میں ان کا دعویٰ ہے کہ ایک بنا جانچے سافٹ ویئر نے 1.3 کروڑ ووٹروں پر 'منطقی تضاد' کا نشان لگایا، 27 لاکھ نام کٹے اور الیکشن کے بعد ٹریبونلوں میں 91 فیصد اپیلیں ووٹر کے حق میں گئیں، پر تب تک ووٹ کا موقع جا چکا تھا۔ 'دراندازوں' کی بات بار بار ہوئی، پر ان کی گنتی کبھی سامنے نہیں آئی۔

الزاموں کی فہرست میں مشین سے پڑھی جا سکنے والی لسٹوں کی جگہ اسکین کی گئی کاپیاں دینا، سچ دکھانے والے صحافیوں پر بہار میں مقدمے، اور راہل گاندھی سے حلف نامہ مانگنا پر انوراگ ٹھاکر کے ایسے ہی دعوے پر چپ رہنا بھی شامل ہے۔
نتیجے میں آنند گیانیش کمار پر غداری کا مقدمہ، ان کی گرفتاری اور 2023 کے تقرری قانون کو رد کرنے کی مانگ کرتے ہیں، جس نے الیکشن کمشنروں کو سرکاری فیصلوں پر قانونی کارروائی سے چھوٹ بھی دے دی۔
nazar: یہ مضمون تحریک کے سب سے تیکھے سُر کا نمونہ ہے، اور اس کے کئی دعوے ابھی الزام ہی ہیں، کسی عدالت کا فیصلہ نہیں۔ پھر بھی اس کا مرکزی سوال جائز ہے: جس ادارے نے کروڑوں لوگوں سے ان کے ہونے کا ثبوت مانگا، وہ اپنے فیصلوں کا ریکارڈ دینے سے کیوں کتراتا ہے؟ بنگال میں 91 فیصد اپیلوں کا ووٹر کے حق میں جانا بتاتا ہے کہ غلطی کا بوجھ کس پر پڑا، غریب اور اقلیتی ووٹر پر، جس نے ووٹ گنوایا اور پھر انصاف کے لیے قطار میں لگا۔
sawal: لاپروائی اور سازش کے بیچ کی لکیر کون کھینچے گا؟

h: Siasat: the questions are for the Commission, so why is the BJP answering?
dek: An editorial in Hyderabad's Urdu daily Siasat says vote theft is now a people's issue, and Amit Shah stepping into the field has increased suspicion, not reduced it.
body: Published on the day of the Ramlila Maidan rally, this Siasat editorial holds that the question of vote theft no longer belongs only to opposition parties. Students, activists, lawyers and civil society are raising it, and public opinion is taking shape. According to the paper, an English daily exposed the allegedly arbitrary and one-sided decisions of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and since then this issue has been at the centre of the national debate.

The editorial's complaint is that the Commission has so far offered no explanation. Reports of differences among the three commissioners came out, but they neither appeared together nor answered the charges. Instead BJP leaders, Union ministers and Chief Ministers came forward to reply, and now Amit Shah too has spoken of running a campaign against the opposition in several states and of a debate or a special session in Parliament.

The paper's argument is simple: the opposition, the young and students are putting their questions not to the government but to the Election Commission. In that case, the BJP answering on the Commission's behalf is beyond its understanding and improper. According to the editorial, every clarification from the BJP deepens the suspicion and raises new questions, because the charge itself is that the Commission's wrong decisions benefited the BJP.

The paper mentions Maharashtra, where by its account about 40 lakh votes were added in the eight months before the Assembly election, and Bengal and Bihar, where lakhs of names were cut and are being restored after the election. The editorial demands that the government stay out and the Commission answer for itself.

The second part of the piece is about rising prices. Everyday goods are going out of reach of ordinary families, and the paper demands action against hoarding. It warns that economic hardship is further fuelling people's anger.
nazar: Siasat has caught a fine but important point: when the ruling party starts answering questions raised about a constitutional body, that itself becomes testimony against the body's independence. This pairing of the Commission's silence and the Home Minister's loudness is the movement's biggest argument.
Linking rising prices to it is not without reason either. The right to vote and the right to bread are not separate fights, and for the readers of an Urdu paper both are part of daily life.
sawal: Why should the Home Minister answer for the Commission's silence?

h: Ravish Kumar: 'regime change' noise is a shield for Gyanesh Kumar
dek: In The Wire Urdu, Ravish Kumar writes that instead of answering questions on vote theft, the government threw the charge of 'regime change' at the opposition so that eyes would not settle on the Chief Election Commissioner.
body: Ravish Kumar says the real 'regime change' is the one in which people are stripped of their right to vote and so denied the very tool for changing a government. In his view the government has given no answer to the charges about SIR and vote theft; instead it turned the debate around by accusing the opposition of a conspiracy to topple the government.

The writer recalls that at first the government stayed silent, then SIR was linked to infiltration. Amit Shah said Rahul Gandhi was protesting to protect infiltrators. Ravish asks how many infiltrators were found in this exercise running since June last year, and why that figure has still not come out, when the Supreme Court had given the Home Ministry the job of examining such cases.

Citing Assam's NRC, he says that more than 1500 crore rupees were spent there, many Hindus were also left out, and once its purpose was served the BJP abandoned it. According to the writer, the same story has now returned through SIR. He claims that if the opposition had not got Aadhaar accepted as a valid document in court, a very large number of people would have been left off the rolls.

He also questions the dismissal of the peaceful Gen Z protests at Jantar Mantar as 'mental Naxalism'. He calls the names cut in Bihar and Bengal an illegal and irreversible loss, and asks why the Commission did not wake up when forms were being filled in bulk.

The article concludes that the 'regime change' row is a curtain to protect Gyanesh Kumar. The Commission itself does not face questions from the press, and a ban at Jantar Mantar will not bring back its credibility. The sense of Ravish's words is that vote theft is an attack on the soul of democracy, and people's attention is being diverted by calling it a ghost.
nazar: This piece is three weeks old, but it feels even truer today: even after Ramlila Maidan, the government's answer is coming not from the Commission but from the Home Minister and BJP leaders. Ravish's sharpest question is the one still unanswered: where is the count of infiltrators?

The comparison with the NRC gives this debate a history. Assam showed that the 'infiltrator' label comes first and the proof never comes, while in between the poorest and weakest are left running after papers.
sawal: Which question is the noise about 'regime change' drowning out?
ref: NRC

National Register of Citizens.
In Assam in 2019, more than 19 lakh people were left out of its final list.
Regime change

The charge of a conspiracy to topple the government.
The BJP has made this charge against the opposition's movement.

h: Local body polls in Pakistan: every government's favourite excuse
dek: A Dawn editorial says provincial governments change the law itself to put off local body elections, and the ordinary citizen pays the price.
body: Pakistan's big parties swear by the Constitution, but shy away from giving people the right to choose the government of their own street and neighbourhood. According to the Dawn editorial, after the emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Article 140-A of the Constitution was suspended first in some districts and then in the whole province, because of which the Election Commission dropped preparations for local body elections there altogether. The term of the previous bodies there ended in June.

The elections due in Islamabad on 20 December are also in limbo, because the delimitation has been challenged in the High Court. Punjab is to vote in February 2027, provided no new obstacle is raised. The law says elections must be held within 120 days of the end of a term, yet Punjab's elections have been due since May 2022 and Islamabad's since June 2021.

The editorial draws attention to a familiar trick: whichever party is in power in a province changes the local government law, so that delimitation is done afresh and the elections slip further. This wastes public money and also keeps people away from their closest representatives.

The paper suggests two remedies. First, the Elections Act 2017 should be amended so that a body's law cannot be changed after its term has ended. Second, the process for local elections should be written clearly into the Constitution itself, so that neither the centre nor the provinces can escape it.

The editorial also reminds readers that strong and accountable local bodies are essential for the development of cities, towns and villages. This is also a democratic alternative to the disputed debate over creating new provinces: that power and money reach the bottom.
nazar: This debate is not Pakistan's alone. In India too, municipal and panchayat (village council) elections have been put off for years in several states, with administrators installed to run things. Where power gathers at the top, the lowest and closest rung of democracy is the first to break. Dawn's suggestion, that the door to changing the rules should be shut, is worth thinking about in both countries.
sawal: Without local government, whose door does democracy reach?
ref: Article 140-A
The provision of Pakistan's Constitution that binds every province to set up local government and hand it political, administrative and financial powers.

h: Nepal: quick decisions are no substitute for accountability
dek: In The Kathmandu Post, a young writer asks why Balen Shah's government avoids questions in Parliament, and where opinions formed by watching reels will take democracy.
body: Nepal's politics these days is fast and dramatic, and the young are watching it more closely than before, but mostly through reels, TikTok and short posts. Law student Ashasvi Karki says this very weakness in information is serving the government. He lists four kinds of supporters: those who accept every claim without checking, those who think being young is a guarantee of being better, people satisfied with quick relief, and blind devotees of Prime Minister Balendra Shah. According to the writer, together they could pave the way for a long 'democratic dictatorship'.

The state of Parliament is a concrete reason for his worry. Rule 56 of the House rules says MPs must get time in the first week of every month to put questions to the Prime Minister. But there is no penalty for not turning up. According to the writer, until the end of July Shah appeared before the House only once, and even after the Speaker's direction in August he stayed mostly absent until the session ended in October, and the Speaker himself is from the ruling party.

There is a question about ordinances too. Article 114 of the Constitution allows an ordinance only when Parliament is not in session and there is an urgent need. The writer alleges that the government summoned Parliament, prorogued it before it could sit and then issued ordinances. About 1,600 political appointees were removed, but key posts were left empty.

Citing an investigation by Kantipur, he says that by the time a hundred days were complete, only 38 of the government's hundred promises had been met. According to the writer, showy steps have left root problems like corruption and brain drain exactly where they were.
The writer's prescription is simple: the Prime Minister should answer in the House, ordinances should come only in a real emergency, and citizens should test a claim before passing it on.
nazar: People had great hopes from the government that came after the Gen Z movement in Nepal. This piece matters because the criticism is coming from within the same generation that demanded change. A new face does not end the need for institutions; answering questions in Parliament is as necessary for any popular leader as it was for the old ones. In South Asia, the mix of charismatic leaders and social media has pushed accountability aside again and again, so this warning should be heard on this side of the border too.
sawal: Should a popular leader be exempt from questions in Parliament?
ref: Article 114
A provision of Nepal's Constitution that allows the government to issue ordinances only when Parliament is not in session and there is an urgent need.
Rule 56
The rule in the rules of Nepal's House of Representatives that sets time in the first week of every month to put questions directly to the Prime Minister.

h: When does a joke become a crime in Turkey?
dek: In Jacobin, Dora Menguc writes that the case against comedian Deniz Goktas shows that in Erdogan's Turkey the limits of laughter are now set by courts and jails.
body: The 32-year-old stand-up comedian Deniz Goktas's hour-and-a-half show 'Olu Deniz' (Dead Sea) was performed 198 times in three years, before more than a lakh of viewers, and no complaint came. The trouble began when he performed it on a big stage in Istanbul and put it on YouTube. Cut-up clips spread and 185 complaints reached the government complaints portal, and Goktas says most of those who complained had not even watched the full show.

On 2 July he was detained at Istanbul airport. The charges were: insulting President Erdogan, inciting hatred and praising a crime. He spent 88 days in a high-security prison, with no sunlight and no talking to other prisoners. On 28 September the court acquitted him of praising a crime, but sentenced him to 11 months and 20 days for insulting the President and seven and a half months for insulting religious values, and then released him.

Goktas argued that calling Erdogan a 'dictator' is a political assessment, not abuse, and that powerful people should put up with jokes. His friend and fellow comedian Emre Gunsal, who was himself jailed in 2020 over a clip, says the real damage is fear: when no one knows where the line is, artists cut their own material before they even write it. According to law professor Tolga Sirin, the crime of incitement arises only when there is a clear and immediate threat to public safety, not from a count of complaints.

The writer links this to a tradition, from 'Markopasa', the satirical paper of Aziz Nesin and Sabahattin Ali, to the Gezi Park movement, on which those in power have laid hands in every age. One line from Goktas tells the whole story: America has cancel culture, we have cancel culture and jail too.
nazar: This story will not seem strange to readers in India. Here too comedians' shows have been cancelled, FIRs (police cases) have been filed against them, and mobs have wrecked stages. The most dangerous thing is what Gunsal says: when the limit is kept blurry, the artist locks his own tongue. Satire is a mirror to power, and a government that fears the mirror really fears its own face.
sawal: What is a power that polices laughter afraid of?
ref: CİMER
The Turkish government's online complaints and petitions portal, through which 185 complaints were lodged against Goktas's show.

h: Riyadh's blasphemy law, Gujarat's cow slaughter law: the same logic
dek: In Scroll, Shoaib Daniyal argues that an India that hands out life sentences for 'insulting' a religious symbol is walking the same road it condemns in Saudi Arabia.
body: Last month a Saudi court sentenced Anojan Sivarasa, a 27-year-old Sri Lankan man, to death for allegedly insulting remarks about Islam and the Prophet. There was an uproar around the world and the sentence was overturned, but he was not acquitted and is still in jail. Against this, Shoaib Daniyal places an Indian verdict of 28 October, in which a court in Gujarat gave three Muslims life imprisonment with hard labour for slaughtering a cow.

According to the writer, the judge drew on the Vedas and the Manusmriti in the verdict, called the cow the pivot of faith and mentioned that 33 crore gods dwell in it. In Gujarat, the punishment for cow slaughter can be as heavy as for murder. The Deputy Chief Minister praised the verdict and supporters celebrated it like a declaration of a 'Hindu Rashtra' (Hindu nation).

After the First World War, Gandhi brought cow protection into national politics, but he favoured persuasion, not punishment. Within two years of his assassination, a ban on cow slaughter entered the Directive Principles of the Constitution, which cannot be enforced in court. Then states made their own laws, and in 2005, with Modi as Chief Minister, Gujarat made a stricter law, which the Supreme Court also upheld.

The writer alleges that after Modi became Prime Minister, mobs repeatedly took Muslim lives in the name of cow protection and these gangs got state protection. He gives the example of Monu Manesar, who is accused of burning two Muslims alive in 2023 but is not in jail.

Daniyal accepts that India is not a monarchy like Saudi Arabia; in 1949 the Constituent Assembly chose the path of making laws by secular reasoning. But his worry is that powerful forces want to reverse that choice. Those who rightly criticise Riyadh's blasphemy law forget that at home they are backing laws just like it.
nazar: This comparison is uncomfortable, but necessary. Protecting the sacred symbol of one religion with the power of the state and punishing other citizens in its name is the true mark of blasphemy laws, whether the symbol is a book or an animal. When a court writes its verdict by quoting scripture and the government celebrates it, the Constitution's secularism stays in the book but not on the ground. The first to pay the price are Muslims, Dalits and the poor who depend on the cattle trade.
sawal: Why does the Constitution's secular promise falter at the court's doorstep?
ref: Directive Principles
The principles in Part IV of the Constitution that guide the government but cannot be enforced through courts; Article 48 speaks of preventing cow slaughter.
photo_note: Purification by muddy water, a satirical drawing by Gaganendranath Tagore

h: Trump lost, but who will stop America's wars?
dek: In Middle East Eye, Sami Al-Arian writes that the Democratic sweep in the midterms is a verdict against the Iran war, but a majority in Congress is not an anti-war majority.
body: In the midterm elections of 3 November, the Democrats won both houses. According to Sami Al-Arian, director of the Center for Islam and Global Affairs at Istanbul Zaim University, they have at least 54 seats in the Senate, seven seats were taken from the Republicans, Kansas elected a Democratic senator for the first time since 1932 and Texas for the first time since 1988.

The writer sees the root of this defeat in the attack on Iran. In the exit polls he cites, 63 percent of voters called the attack wrong, 87 percent were troubled by fuel prices and only 38 percent were happy with Trump's work. Because of the disruption in Hormuz, petrol reached about 4.27 dollars a gallon by the end of October. Vice President Vance blamed the defeat squarely on the war. He takes the win in Michigan of Abdul El-Sayed, who spoke openly on Gaza, and the win in Texas of James Talarico, who refused AIPAC money, as proof of this shift.

But Al-Arian warns against wishful thinking. It was the Biden government that gave Israel weapons in the Gaza war and vetoed ceasefire resolutions at the United Nations. Citing Brown University's 'Costs of War' project, he says that in the two years after 7 October 2023, the US gave Israel at least 21.7 billion dollars in military aid. At least 11 newly elected members support Palestinian rights, yet the party leadership treats Israel as a central ally.

From January the new Congress can rein in the war and arms sales through investigations, subpoenas and budget conditions, but it does not have the two-thirds majority needed to override a veto. There is also the fear that the outgoing Congress will lock in a huge military budget for Israel before then. His bottom line is that electoral change is not structural change; the structure that sustains the wars is still standing in its place.
nazar: The American voter has said clearly that he does not want to pay for distant wars out of his own pocket. But history shows that in Washington war policy has been the shared estate of both parties. The real test will be whether the new Congress only corners Trump or also breaks the consensus that led to the destruction in Gaza and Iran. For the Global South this is not just America's internal matter, because the closing of Hormuz has hit the prices of oil and fertiliser from Delhi to Dhaka.
sawal: Can voters' anger change the direction of the war machine?
ref: AIPAC
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a powerful pro-Israel lobby that spends heavily for and against candidates in US elections.
Lame-duck session
Meetings of the old Congress after the election and before the new Congress is sworn in, in which members who lost also vote.
photo_note: Snow Storm: Hannibal and his Army Crossing the Alps

h: Netanyahu's decline and Modi's Israeli bet
dek: In The Federal, D Ravi Kanth asks where India's diplomacy and morality will stand once the leader Modi grew so close to leaves power.
body: In last month's election in Israel, no party won a majority of 60 seats. On 7 November President Isaac Herzog invited Gadi Eisenkot to form the government; his broad coalition has outside support from the Arab-Palestinian parties with 19 seats. Eisenkot rejected Netanyahu's offer of a 'unity government' and said his aim is to remove the leader responsible for the failure of 7 October 2023. Netanyahu blamed Qatar for the Arab parties' win.

D Ravi Kanth recalls that Netanyahu, hemmed in by an International Criminal Court arrest warrant and corruption cases, has been among Modi's closest foreign friends. He had invited Modi to Israel's 2027 Independence Day celebrations, and on 28 February, two days before the attack on Iran, the Israeli parliament honoured Modi. The writer calls that war illegal and asks whether the invitation still stands.

Netanyahu's troubles lie outside home too. According to the writer, Trump announced that the military aid of about 4 billion dollars a year to Israel will end by the end of this year, two years before the current agreement expires, and Herzog said he had not even had a hint of it. In September, when Netanyahu spoke at the UN General Assembly, most countries got up and walked out.

The writer's criticism of India is sharp. Modi at once called the killing of seven Israelis in Tel Aviv 'heinous', but stayed silent on the deaths of Palestinian civilians and the destruction in Gaza. The RSS invited the Israeli ambassador to its hundredth foundation day event. India is a signatory to the 1948 Genocide Convention, while the International Court of Justice is hearing genocide charges against Israel; in the writer's opinion, a new bilateral investment treaty with Israel could be treated as complicity under international law.
nazar: This is the risk of resting foreign policy on one leader's personal friendship: the leader goes, but the stain of standing with him stays. For decades India raised its voice for Palestinian rights, and that credibility was its capital in the Global South. Silence on Gaza and closeness in a time of war have reduced that capital. If power is changing in Israel itself, this is a chance for Delhi to return to its old, principled line.
sawal: In the diplomacy of friendship, where is the room left for principles?
ref: Genocide Convention (1948)
The UN convention that treats genocide as an international crime and obliges signatory countries to prevent it and to avoid taking part in it.

h: Showing violence at a procession is not spreading enmity: FIR against journalist quashed
dek: The Madhya Pradesh High Court ended the case against Raisen YouTube journalist Uvesh Khan, saying that reporting a clash is not in itself a crime.
body: In Silwani town of Raisen district, fights broke out at two places during the Ganesh immersion on 6 September last year. At about nine at night a man was hit on the head with a stick, and a second clash took place near a Shiva temple close by. Independent journalist Uvesh Khan, who runs a channel called 'Uvesh Reporter', posted a video of it. A big TV channel had also shown the same incident, and its report said CCTV footage showed police standing and watching.

The next day Khan got phone calls asking him to remove the video, and he did remove it. Even so, on 8 September an FIR (police case) was filed against him under Section 196(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita on a complaint by a man named Rajeev Soni. The complaint said the video's title, which spoke of a 'bloody clash' and two people seriously injured, spread fear and confusion among the Hindu community.

In an order of 28 October, Justice Himanshu Joshi quashed the case. Citing earlier Supreme Court rulings, the court said an offence under this section arises only when there is an intent to incite enmity between at least two communities. The feelings of one community being stirred is not enough. The FIR did not point to even a single word that incited enmity.

The court also held that the mere fact that a news report concerns a sensitive incident cannot curb free speech, and that continuing the case would be an abuse of legal process. According to Alt News, Khan's reach fell after the FIR, and one source says the same news ran in many other places that day, but he alone was targeted.
nazar: YouTube journalists in small towns are often alone, with no institution to lean on and no team of lawyers. One complaint and one section can stop their work for months. The High Court's ruling is a relief, but the process itself has already become the punishment: a fourteen-month case and a shrinking livelihood. There is also the question of why, when a big channel showed the same incident, only Uvesh Khan was charged.
sawal: One story, many channels: why was only Uvesh charged?
ref: Section 196 of the Nyaya Sanhita

This section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita has replaced Section 153A of the old IPC.
It makes spreading enmity between groups on grounds of religion, caste or language a crime.

h: Supreme Court on Delhi's air: bans alone will not work
dek: At the pollution hearing the court asked for reports instead of giving directions, and set aside a doctor's view on children's lungs as anecdote.
body: In the case it started on its own on pollution in Delhi-NCR, the bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana signalled that the court's role should stay limited, because too many orders only encourage violations. The bench suggested that awareness of pollution be built into the Diwali celebrations themselves, with councillors and neighbourhood committees appealing to people not to create smoke.

A chest surgeon from Ganga Ram Hospital said that the lungs of Delhi's children are not healthy. The bench said it would go not by such personal opinions but by expert bodies and the recommendations of GRAP, unless some peer-reviewed research said otherwise. A lawyer cited a 2012 study which found the lung capacity of schoolchildren to be 43.5 percent lower. Justice Bagchi also opposed closing schools, listing the weaknesses of online classes.

Amicus curiae Aparajita Singh said the air was close to the 'severe' category and that stubble burning made up 14 percent of the pollution up to 5 November. She argued that the subsidised machines are costly to run and of no use on small farms. The Chief Justice suggested giving the machines to panchayats (village councils) and fixing the purchase rate in advance.

On the issue of vehicles waiting at the border with their engines running, the Additional Solicitor General admitted that earlier orders had not been fully implemented. The Centre said diesel autos would be phased out by 1 January 2027. In the end, the bench asked officials for reports instead of giving any directions.
nazar: The court's remark that bans do not work is both honest and worrying. When the AQI is touching 400 and the amicus is pointing out that the city average hides the poison in each street, accepting 'poor' air as normal is the biggest defeat. The price is paid by children who play outdoors and by workers who labour on the roads, who have neither an air purifier nor the leave to stay at home.
sawal: How much smoke will it take for the evidence of children's lungs to count as proof?
ref: GRAP

The Graded Response Action Plan, a plan of step-by-step restrictions based on the state of the air.
It is enforced by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM).

h: Mosques of Barmer and Jaisalmer: a hearing must come before the bulldozer
dek: The Jodhpur bench of the Rajasthan High Court said structures cannot be demolished without hearing the reply to a notice and without a written, reasoned order.
body: On 6 November the Jodhpur bench of the High Court passed an important order on the bulldozer drive against mosques and mazars (shrines) in Rajasthan's border districts. Hearing five appeals, the bench of Justice Vineet Kumar Mathur and Justice Chandrashekhar Sharma said that affected people must get a full and fair chance to put their case.

The main case was Gafoor vs State of Rajasthan. Lawyers for the appellants argued that the administration was demolishing structures without taking and considering replies to show cause notices. The government assured that nothing would be demolished until the notice proceedings were decided. The court asked the appellants to file detailed replies within two weeks, after which the officer must hold a hearing, examine all the documents and pass a written, reasoned order.

On the basis of this order, appeals relating to two mosques in Barmer and to the Pokaran area of Jaisalmer were also disposed of. According to Jamiat Ulama-e-Rajasthan, the drive began on 18 June and fourteen mosques and mazars have already been demolished. On 13 July the High Court had dismissed more than forty petitions, after which the Supreme Court imposed a fifteen-day interim stay and opened the way for an appeal before a division bench.

The Jamiat alleges that one of its delegations was stopped from visiting the affected areas. A second team that went in October says these mosques were built by villagers themselves in remote sandy areas. A large part of the report rests on the Jamiat's press release, and the government's side is not in it.
nazar: This order says nothing new. It only repeats what lies at the foundation of law: first listen, then decide. But when fourteen places of worship have already fallen, this reminder is relief that came late. For the desert villages that built these mosques with their own hands, the real test comes now, when we see whether the officer truly hears them or only goes through the ritual.
sawal: Who will give a hearing to the fourteen places of worship that have already fallen?
ref: Show cause notice

A notice sent to the affected party before any action is taken.
It asks why the action should not be taken, and the reply must be considered.

h: How were power and water cut without notice? High Court on Race Course mosque
dek: On an appeal about a waqf and heritage-listed mosque near the Prime Minister's residence, the Delhi High Court sought replies from the NDMC and the Waqf Board.
body: On Friday the Delhi High Court raised questions over the cutting of electricity and water to the Race Course mosque, which stands inside the Race Course Club in New Delhi. During the hearing Justice Subramonium Prasad said plainly that electricity cannot be cut without notice, especially when the building is a notified property.

The appeal has been filed by the mosque's imam, Mohammad Haroon, against a 15 October order of a single judge who had refused to restore the services. The bench of Justice Prasad and Justice Renu Bhatnagar issued notice to the New Delhi Municipal Council and the Delhi Waqf Board and sought their replies within two weeks. The next hearing will be on 14 December.

The imam's lawyer, M. Sufian Siddiqui, argued that officials had relied on a judgment in a different case, which concerned encroachment by three slum settlements opposite the Prime Minister's residence and in which the mosque was not even a party. After that judgment, about seven hundred families were evicted in August. According to the appeal, the real question is whether the council has the right to stop power and water to a working mosque and its hujra, and the single judge's order rests on a wrong reading of waqf law.

The mosque has been listed since 2009 as waqf property and as a Grade II heritage building. The Centre is running a drive to take back this land of the roughly 53-acre club. On 29 October the Centre told the court that it would decide the Waqf Board's application within four weeks and that there would be no coercive action until then. Meanwhile, the Centre has also told the court that it intends to remove the old Qadimi mosque in the Krishi Bhawan complex.
nazar: Cutting off a building's lights and water before tearing it down is an old method: the bulldozer comes later, but the uprooting begins first. If this is happening to a heritage mosque in the area closest to power, think what must happen in faraway settlements. The court's question is right, but while waiting for answers the mosque will stay in the dark until December.
sawal: How many days will heritage status protect a building once its lights go out?
ref: Hujra

A small room attached to a mosque, where the imam or muezzin usually lives.
In this case, the cutting of its electricity has been challenged.

h: NoCap's Facebook page will return; government says it never asked for a block
dek: In the Kerala High Court the government admitted it had only asked for some comments to be removed, yet a Malayalam news page stayed shut in India for five weeks.
body: The Facebook page of the Malayalam digital news platform NoCap stopped being visible in India on 28 September. Meta said this was done under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, on a notice from the central government or some legal agency. Chief editor Haider Ali K. went to the High Court. He said the blocking order was neither made public nor shared with him.

The petition sought that the order and related papers be produced in court, that the order be stayed, and that the page be restored while the case went on. It also raised the question of where transparency and procedural safeguards are in such actions to block content. At the first hearing on 26 October, the court asked both the Centre and the Kerala government whether either of them had asked for the page to be blocked, and also issued notice to Meta.

The government lawyer replied that Meta had only been asked to remove some comments under some posts, and there was no direction to shut the whole page. Relying on this statement, Justice Ziyad Rahman A.A. ordered on 5 November that the page could run again after removing the comments flagged by the State Police Chief or officers under him, and that Meta would take the necessary steps.
According to SFLC.in, the organisation helping NoCap, the block badly hit both the platform's reach and its earnings, though the report does not give figures for the loss.
nazar: This case shows how blurry censorship has become today. The government says it did not ask for the page to be shut, the company says it shut it on the government's notice, and in between a small news platform stays cut off from its readers for five weeks. When orders stay hidden and no one is responsible, the loss always falls on the one asking questions.
sawal: Who will pay damages for an order that nobody gave?
ref: IT Act Section 79(3)(b)

This section obliges platforms to remove unlawful content once they receive notice from the government.
If they do not, they can lose their legal protection from liability for users' content.

h: Three thousand kilometres in nine days: the elephants' journey from Assam to temples
dek: The Supreme Court voiced concern over the haste with which elephants were sent from Assam to Tamil Nadu, but said they cannot now be put through the ordeal of being sent back.
body: On 5 November the bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi expressed deep concern in the case of captive elephants sent from Assam to Tamil Nadu. A petition by the organisation People for Cattle in India alleges that the set legal process was bypassed in sending these elephants. This report is by The Wire and was published by The News Minute.

Senior advocate Meenakshi Arora, for the petitioner, said such a transfer involves several rounds of checks, approvals and consultations, which usually take at least fifty days. Here the application was made on 4 September and the elephant reached Chennai by 13 September, meaning a journey of about three thousand kilometres in nine days. She also placed before the court a table with the date of each approval.

At the centre is Durga, a five-year-old female elephant, handed over to the Meenakshi Amman temple in Madurai. According to the report, a religious organisation named Seva Trust 'gifted' her, and gave four more young elephants to temples in Nagapattinam, Kanchipuram and Tiruvannamalai. The trust is run by the wife of a man whom an earlier investigation by The News Minute described as close to senior central leaders.

The bench accepted that all the elephants have already been sent and cannot be put through the hardship of being returned. The Chief Justice said that if the matter had come to light earlier, the court would have stepped in. The bench also repeated that no High Court or state government can go against its directions in force since 2021, which cover the identification of captive elephants, checks on ownership and audits of their transport.
nazar: An elephant is not a gift box to be sent from one corner of the country to another in nine days on the strength of influence. The court's helplessness also stings: the rules were broken, yet the outcome cannot be reversed, because putting the animal through the same ordeal again would be a greater cruelty. When haste itself becomes the defence, the law will always stay one step behind.
sawal: On whose word did a fifty-day approval come through in nine days?
ref: Transfer of captive elephants

Under the Wildlife Protection Act, moving a captive elephant from one state to another needs written approval from the Chief Wildlife Warden.
The Supreme Court has been monitoring this since 2021.

h: The Virudhunagar blast: a holiday's wages that cost lives
dek: A Sunday explosion at a firecracker factory in Tamil Nadu killed 25 workers, 21 of them women. PARI's photographer spoke to the families left behind.
body: 19 April 2026 was a Sunday. The rules say firecracker units must stay shut on holidays, yet work was going on at the Vanaja Firecracker factory near Kattanarpatti village in Virudhunagar district. Work with gunpowder that should be finished by nine in the morning went on until three in the afternoon on that scorching day. The blast killed 25 people. PARI photographer M. Palani Kumar went to the homes whose people never came back.

Of the dead, 21 were women. Most had come for the extra Sunday wages and a cash bonus, because two days of election holidays lay ahead, and one had a loan to repay, another had fees to pay, another needed money for medicines. Of the 25, 19 were from the Mutharaiyar community and six were Dalits. Nineteen of them came from the same village.

The families' accounts paint a similar picture: a sick or disabled husband, children still in school, and a mother running the home who had been in this work for twenty-five or thirty years. Fourteen-year-old Jayamurugan lost both his parents. Farming depends on the rain and water is scarce, so even graduates here work in firecrackers.

Workers explain why accidents happen: mixing more chemicals than needed, storing and mixing gunpowder in the same place, twenty or thirty people in a room meant for four. News of inspections arrives in advance. According to the report, the factory's licence was suspended, yet work continued.

The government gave each family 5.5 lakh rupees and the Fireworks Manufacturers Association gave three lakh rupees. Bhimrao of the Dalit Liberation Movement points out that in a 2021 blast the National Green Tribunal had ordered 20 lakh for each bereaved family, and the same amount should be paid now. By his count, around 22 blasts in 11 years have killed about 384 workers, the largest share of them from Scheduled Castes, while the industry is worth more than six thousand crore rupees a year.
nazar: The light that spreads across the sky every Diwali is paid for by the women of Virudhunagar with their lives, and that price is never added to any bill. The rules exist, but this report makes clear that the system meant to enforce them either arrives late or sends word in advance.

The families' demands are very modest: some support in the summer months, work ending early in the morning, strict monitoring. In an industry where most of the dead are women from Dalit and backward castes, ignoring safety is not just negligence but also a social choice.
sawal: Whose life burns in the light of a firecracker?
ref: National Green Tribunal (NGT)
A special tribunal set up for environmental cases. In the 2021 Achankulam blast it took up the matter on its own and ordered 20 lakh rupees for the families of the dead.
Sivakasi-Virudhunagar
The region of Tamil Nadu where most of the country's firecrackers are made. Because farming here is dry, a large part of the village population depends on this work.

h: A loan of one lakh, fifty lakh repaid, and a kidney
dek: Roshan Kule, a farmer from Minthur village in Chandrapur, borrowed money to treat his sick cows. The first part of a three-part PARI series shows how that loan became a trap.
body: March 2021, the second wave of Covid. Lumpy skin disease struck the twelve Jersey cows of Roshan Kule, a small farmer in Minthur village of Chandrapur district. Six cows died and his milk income of about 80 thousand rupees a month stopped. Getting a bank loan was hard, so he borrowed one lakh rupees from a private moneylender in Brahmapuri.

Roshan alleges that the moneylender set the terms of repayment within fifteen days, twenty percent interest and a fine of five thousand rupees a day, and that he was beaten when he objected. He was then passed from one moneylender to another, and, he says, forced to take loans from cooperative societies, microfinance companies and banks too.

Based on diaries and bank accounts, investigators have accepted that Roshan paid back about fifty lakh rupees, while he himself puts it at 72 to 75 lakh. The house is mortgaged to four lenders, the gold is gone, the tractor was seized, and the four acres of land his father bought were sold for a pittance. Many nights the family went to bed hungry.

In 2024, looking for a way out of the pressure, Roshan reached a kidney-selling gang through Facebook and went to Cambodia to sell his kidney. In 2025 he was taken to scam compounds in Laos, from where he was rescued. In November 2025 his wife Rohini attempted suicide. The next day the family's story ran on a local TV channel, and only then was an FIR registered.

The police have filed a preliminary chargesheet of about six thousand pages. The investigation found that none of the six moneylenders was registered. Arrested in December 2025, these moneylenders are now out on bail. The family now lives on Rohini's anganwadi (village childcare centre) salary of 7,500 rupees, Roshan's father's pension and his brother's daily wages, and a large part of the salary goes in instalments.
nazar: Several committees on farmer suicides in Vidarbha have said that the moneylending system running parallel to the banks is a major cause, yet this debt barely shows up in government data. Roshan's story shows that when formal credit is not available at the time of need, even a sick cow can sink an entire family.
This is not just one farmer's misfortune but the failure of a system in which illegal moneylenders operate without fear for years and the police act only when a camera arrives.
sawal: Why does a farmer find a moneylender before a bank?
ref: Lumpy skin disease
A viral disease of cattle that causes lumps on the body and lowers milk yield. In 2020-22 it affected lakhs of animals in many states of the country.
The Minthur series
Jaideep Hardikar's three-part report on PARI. This first part is the story of the debt; later parts go on to the kidney sale and the scam compounds of Laos.

h: Mango orchards cut, land leased for 33 years, a 10x12 room in return
dek: In Pirpainti, Bhagalpur, 479 hectares have been leased to Adani Power for 33 years. Sixty-eight Adivasi families are being given one room each, and they do not appear in the papers at all.
body: In Pirpainti in Bhagalpur district, a hundred metres from the road, is Santhal Tola, a hamlet of about a dozen Santhal Adivasi homes. Day and night there is the sound of hundreds of trucks reversing and the rumble of bulldozers. Sunil Soren, 51, complains first that he cannot sleep. Then he says the real trouble is bigger: a 2,400-megawatt thermal plant is coming up here, and it takes away both his home and his farm labour. The land has gone to Adani Power; work began early in 2026.

The 479 hectares were leased to Adani Power Ltd for 33 years in August 2025, two months before the Bihar election. Of this, 400 hectares is private land and 79 hectares government land. Santhal and Sauria Paharia families have lived on this 'private' land for generations but have no papers in their names. The villagers knew nothing until landowners began receiving money in December 2025. The Adani group's environmental impact assessment report does not mention Adivasis at all, so there is no rehabilitation or compensation plan either.

The public hearing was held in January 2026. Riju Paharia heard of it from others; he went with dozens of people and gave the block development officer a letter about their fears, but his name is not in the attendance register. Of the 68 families to be displaced, 52 are Sauria Paharia, who belong to a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, and 16 are Santhal. The government document prepared after the hearing carries 447 signatures, among them a couple of Sauria Paharia and not one Santhal. The people who had been speaking against the project were held under Section 126 of the BNS from nine in the morning till five in the evening the day before the hearing, and were released only after it was over.

For rehabilitation, 71 rooms are being built five kilometres away on land leased to the company, each 10 by 12 feet with a small kitchen. Adivasis allege the rooms have no pillars and the roof is asbestos; a contractor said they were building to the size the company had given, though the reporter could not verify this independently. Sanjhli Marandi has three large rooms and six goats and chickens, and asks how all of it will fit into one room. The block development officer says ownership will be given and that mutation has been done.

Livelihood went with it. The orchards gave people work all year, 400 to 700 rupees a day. According to the report, lakhs of mango and other fruit trees have been uprooted in less than a year; a timber bid document mentions three lakh trees across 400 acres, while Shravan Singh's petition to the National Green Tribunal claims five to ten lakh fruit-bearing trees, including five lakh mango trees 25 to 30 years old. People say the water table has also fallen since the digging began.
nazar: Everything is in the papers except the Adivasis: the environmental impact assessment does not mention them, the hearing document does not carry their signatures, and on the day of the hearing they were held in detention. Consent was not built, it was only entered on paper.

Adivasis are 1.5 per cent of Bihar's population, so they are politically invisible and helpless before the administration and the company. Set 71 rooms against 479 hectares and a 33-year lease, and it is clear whose side the bargain favours.
sawal: Why is a ten-by-twelve room enough in place of an orchard that shaded three generations?
ref: Sauria Paharia
A Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group of Bihar; their population in the state is about 7,444. They make up most of the families to be displaced in Pirpainti.
Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)
The study required before a big project, which must account for its effect on land, water, air and the people living there, and is followed by a public hearing.
photo_note: Symbolic photo: a mango orchard in Bihar

h: Lions on the Tigris: a doorframe that survived Mosul's rubble
dek: Zardasht Ahmed's film on Al Jazeera Witness uses three men in post-ISIL Mosul to ask who owns the heritage of a ruined city.
body: The Iraqi city of Mosul lies on the banks of the Tigris river, and its history is thought to go back some eight thousand years. From 2014 to 2017 the city was held by ISIL, and in the battle to free it a large part of the old city was turned to rubble. Zardasht Ahmed's film, shown on Al Jazeera's Witness programme, begins its story with a marble doorframe standing amid this rubble, with two lions carved above it.

This doorframe is the only surviving part of Bashar's family home. Bashar is a fisherman by trade, and his large ancestral house collapsed in the battle to liberate Mosul. Now he guards this doorway, as if everything that went with the house had survived in this stone.

The second character is Fakhri, a former soldier who collects old objects in his passion to save the city's heritage. He has an informal museum of his own and wants this lion doorframe to go there. A large part of the film rests on the long conversations and bargaining between Bashar and Fakhri over this doorframe.

The third character is Fadhil, Fakhri's friend and a violinist. Under ISIL rule music was banned and artists like Fadhil had their voices taken away. Now he wants to bring melody back to the city. According to the film's introduction, it is he who reminds Fakhri that behind every old object lies some person's loss.

In this way the film takes the question of heritage out of bookish debate and into everyday life: is a broken home one family's memory or the whole city's heritage? Is displaying it in a museum saving it, or taking away someone's last support? The lions on the doorframe become, in the film, signs of both stubbornness and cultural survival.

Zardasht Ahmed wrote, directed and shot the film himself. It is a joint production of Norway and the Netherlands, with archival material from an Iraqi company. The film had its world premiere in 2025 in the human rights competition of the CPH:DOX festival in Copenhagen, and received a special mention at Armenia's Golden Apricot film festival.
nazar: News from cities after war often shrinks to counts of buildings and reconstruction budgets. This film reminds us that heritage is not only stone but also the memory of those whose homes were destroyed. Taking away an ordinary person's last support in the name of saving culture is also a kind of dispossession.
Here too, from Ayodhya to Banaras, old neighbourhoods have been torn down in the name of heritage and beautification. Bashar of Mosul makes us ask for whom heritage is saved, and who pays its price.
sawal: Whose home is at stake in saving heritage?
ref: Mosul
A large city in northern Iraq on the banks of the Tigris. It was held by ISIL from 2014 to 2017, and the old city was badly destroyed in the battle to free it.
Witness
Al Jazeera English's documentary programme, which shows films by independent filmmakers from around the world about the lives of ordinary people.

h: Stones falling from a rooftop and a girl's 'cholera' death
dek: In the tenth instalment of the series 'Mritatmaon ka Desh', Neha Naruka tells the story of a small town's rooftop, a bold girl and her death that was quietly buried.
body: Neha Naruka's series of death stories on Sammukh, 'Mritatmaon ka Desh' (Land of the Dead Souls), has reached its tenth instalment. At the start the writer asks herself what is new in such stories when newspapers are full of such news every day. She thinks lightly about paths like research papers, a job in advertising or giving up writing, and in the end chooses to keep writing.

At the centre of the story is a girl from the neighbourhood whom the writer calls Chhammakchhallo (a teasing name for a flirtatious girl). She threw stones from the rooftop into neighbours' courtyards and, when caught, blamed her brother. Her family would lock the door to the roof, but she always got up there on the excuse of drying clothes or checking the water tank. One stone fell near the writer too, and the old women sitting in the courtyard passed judgement on the girl's 'ways'.

Then the story suddenly descends into darkness. According to the writer, the girl's mother had advised her to stay at home, she did not listen, and her father took her life. In the neighbourhood it was called a death from cholera. Some time later the father also died, and people linked it to the curse of killing a daughter.

The writer opens another thread: in the house where the most stones fell, there was a boy who studied on the roof, who disappeared that same day and later returned with a government job and marriage offers with dowry. She treats this as gossip too, and also imagines that the stones may have been aimed at him. The real truth, according to her, was known only to the father.

Against this she sets another episode from the neighbourhood, where a boy who made obscene gestures at women from a rooftop was let off with 'boys will be boys'. People advised the father, who kept a gun, to go into politics. This irony hangs over the whole piece.
nazar: Naruka's prose moves in the language of jokes and banter and suddenly comes to rest on a death that the whole neighbourhood forgot by calling it an illness. It is this almost careless tone that unsettles the reader more.
In our view this piece says more than any report on 'honour killing': a woman's desire is a crime, a man's misbehaviour is his 'nature', and the man who commits violence sees a future in politics.
sawal: Which death does a neighbourhood forget by calling it an illness, and why?
ref: Mritatmaon ka Desh
Neha Naruka's series of death stories on Sammukh, in which the nameless deaths of small-town life are recorded through a mix of memoir and fiction.
Neha Naruka

Hindi poet, author of the poetry collection 'Phati Hatheliyan' (Cracked Palms).
According to Sammukh's author note, she received the 2024 Vagishwari Samman.

h: In a marriage, where does self-respect end and ego begin
dek: In the fifth instalment of her column 'Dampatya', Pallavi Vinod uses stories from three homes to show how patriarchy feeds ego and hollows out a relationship.
body: Pallavi Vinod's column 'Dampatya' (Married Life) on Sammukh looks at marriage apart from the romantic glow of rituals. In the fifth instalment, her opening point is simple: a good life partner is one who shares the everyday load, laughs together over small things and is a support in hard times.

The essay turns on the difference between self-respect and ego. According to the writer, self-respect protects oneself but does not hurt the partner, while ego is a hard shell that wounds everyone who comes close. Ego is born of inner frustration, self-respect of good intent, and it includes respect for others too.

She links this directly to patriarchy, which builds a ladder of ruler and ruled within the same family and places money and power above other contributions, while a home runs on love, care, time and earnings alike. Drawing on Kabir's famous saying that 'I' and love cannot live together, she says this is easy to understand and hard to live by.

Three stories make the debate concrete. In one, a wife from a rich home constantly mocks her husband's modest family, and years later the daughter is cut off from her grandparents. In the second, a mother-in-law praised for social work during Covid discriminates against her sick daughter-in-law. In the third, a husband slaps his wife after a minor argument at a film theatre in which she turned out to be right; years later she recognises his behaviour as signs of narcissistic personality disorder.

The writer also accepts that women too taunt and insult, for instance over a husband's earnings or his family responsibilities. At the end she asks the reader to look within: if your partner is suffocating because of your behaviour, you have failed as a human being.
nazar: This essay can also be read as a sermon, but its strength lies in its stories, which break the habit of brushing off domestic violence and humiliation as 'a matter between husband and wife'.
In our view the most important point is that the writer sees ego not as a personal flaw but as a product of the structure of power. Equality inside the home is also a question of democracy.
sawal: With what conversation should equality inside the home begin?
ref: Narcissistic personality disorder
A mental condition in which a person sees himself as exceptional, craves praise and cares little for others' feelings.
Kabir
A 15th-century saint-poet whose couplets are known for striking at ego, hypocrisy and caste.

h: 'Gondhal': where a folk ritual itself becomes a character in the story
dek: Vani Tripathi Tikoo reviews the Marathi film chosen as India's official entry for the Oscars, praising it while also warning against hasty celebration.
body: On Janaki Pul, actor, theatre artist and writer Vani Tripathi Tikoo has written at length on Santosh Davakhar's Marathi film 'Gondhal'. According to her, the Film Federation of India chose it from 33 films as India's official entry in the International Feature Film category of the 99th Academy Awards. She makes clear that this is a selection, not a nomination.

Gondhal is a folk-religious performance of Maharashtra, linked to the worship of Bhavani and Khandoba. At weddings and auspicious occasions, Gondhali artists seek the goddess's blessing through a whole night of song, dance, drama and storytelling. According to the review, this tradition has also been a way of passing myths, local history and social values from generation to generation.

The film tells the story of Suman (Ishita Deshmukh), trapped in a stifling marriage with her wealthy husband Anand, while her heart is drawn to the Gondhali artist Sahiba. Anand's cousin Sarjerao is infatuated with Suman, and Suman turns his obsession into a conspiracy that goes as far as a plan for murder. On the night of the gondhal, the lines between performance and reality, devotion and deceit begin to blur. Above it all hangs the shadow of the feudal headman Abasaheb Patil.

What draws the writer most is that Suman is neither a helpless victim nor a simple villain; she makes deliberate choices and wants to take back control of her life through relationships. The ritual here is not a backdrop but part of the plot. The film also asks how a society that celebrates devotion puts up with injustice.

The review also puts a rein on the celebration. The writer reminds us that after 'Shwaas', 'Harishchandrachi Factory' and 'Court', this is the fourth Marathi entry, and India has never won. Instead of selling folk culture as a 'curiosity' to foreign audiences, the film should first be judged as cinema, and the country should present its many voices with confidence.
nazar: This review is valuable because it looks at the film outside the frame of Hindi, star-led 'representative cinema', and treats folk tradition not as decoration but as a stage for a debate on power and desire.
In our view its warning against the habit of turning the Oscar race into a 'national victory' is just as important.
sawal: Do films made on folk traditions reach their own audiences?
ref: Gondhal
A folk-religious performance of Maharashtra in which Gondhali artists sing, dance and tell stories all night in praise of Bhavani and Khandoba.
Waghya-Murali
Male (waghya) and female (murali) devotee-performers of the Khandoba tradition, who have taken part in folk songs and night-long devotional gatherings.

h: The 'anti-library' president who broke a hundred-year tradition
dek: Information science professor Alex Poole has combed through the statements of seventeen US presidents to show how Donald Trump stands apart when it comes to libraries.
body: In Dawn's 'Books & Authors', the essay by Alex H. Poole, associate professor at Drexel University, begins with a statement of 31 March 2026, when Trump said his presidential library would probably be a hotel with Air Force One in its lobby, and also that he does not believe in building a library or a museum.

Poole has read the speeches, government papers and American Library Association material of seventeen presidents from 1923 to now. According to him, presidents of both parties have called libraries the foundation of democracy and informed citizenship. Roosevelt warned against leaders who want to decide what the public reads; Eisenhower spoke against censorship during the 'Red Scare' and signed a law for rural libraries; Kennedy said libraries should be open to all except the censor.

This line runs through Reagan, Clinton, Obama and Biden. Obama called libraries a means of separating truth from falsehood and opposed book bans; Biden called library services essential in a 2022 executive order.

Trump breaks from this tradition. The writer lists how in 2019 he mocked Narendra Modi's claim of building a library in Afghanistan; at the start of his second term the Education Department post that monitored book bans was abolished; and in March 2025 came an order to abolish the federal agency that funds libraries and museums, which a court blocked.

In May 2025 Librarian of Congress Carla Hayden was removed, the first woman and the first African American to hold the post; the reasons listed included 'DEI' and 'inappropriate books' for children. The essay ends with a September 2026 speech in which Trump accused opposition candidates of wanting to fill children's libraries with books by Lenin and Stalin.
nazar: This essay builds no grand theory. It simply lays out the documents in order, and that order becomes the strongest argument: an attack on libraries is really an attack on the public's right to know.
In our view there is a mirror here for the Indian reader too, where chapters are dropped from the syllabus and books are blocked in the name of 'hurt sentiments'.
sawal: When did you last check the state of the public library in your town?
ref: Institute of Museum and Library Services
A US federal agency, the largest government body giving grants to libraries and museums across the country.
Red Scare
The anti-communist frenzy in the US in the 1950s, in which writers, teachers and books were targeted on suspicion of 'treason'.

h: From Almora to Heidelberg: unseen threads of the freedom struggle
dek: Divya Aslesha reviews Devaki Pande's first novel 'The Imitation Englishman', which sees the era of the Ghadar movement and the Hindu-German Conspiracy through the eyes of a young man.
body: On Scroll, Divya Aslesha has reviewed Devaki Pande's first novel 'The Imitation Englishman' (Bloomsbury India). The story begins in 1916, when twenty-year-old Madhusudan of Almora goes to Heidelberg in Germany to study law, while his elder brother, now a soldier, is being sent to North Africa in the First World War.

On the sea voyage he meets Amir Farooqui of Rawalpindi, who is linked to the Hindu-German Conspiracy gathering weapons for a revolt against British rule. In Germany, the beating of soldiers in a bar sharpens Madhusudan's political understanding. Amir goes to America, joins the Ghadar movement and is killed during the San Francisco trial; Madhusudan reaches London, where he faces racism at a fictional university, forms an Indian Association and finally returns as a lawyer, having lost his brother and his dreams to the empire.

According to the reviewer, the novel's strength is that it does not see the freedom struggle in a single colour. It has armed revolutionaries, big leaders, people who stood with the British and also those who hollowed out the Raj from within. Its eye on race and class in London is sharp, especially on the rich Indian friends busy becoming 'imitation Englishmen'.

But the flaws listed are no fewer. The two parts feel like two separate stories, at the start Amir's character overshadows the hero, the conspiracy thread is dropped as soon as the story reaches London, the early prose and dialogue are artificial, and the balance between history and story wobbles. The reviewer also notes that despite an upper-caste hero, the novel avoids the question of caste.
Even so, she found the book fast-paced and relevant, especially in October, when protests across the country were borrowing the language of the freedom struggle.
nazar: This review honestly weighs the novel's merits and faults. The most interesting thing is that it puts a finger on the absence of caste, an old silence in most stories of the freedom struggle.

In our view, bringing the forgotten stories of Ghadar and the émigré revolutionaries back into fiction is important work in itself, especially when the push to fit the history of independence into a single mould is growing.
sawal: Why is caste so rarely seen in stories of the freedom struggle?
ref: Ghadar movement
A revolutionary movement begun in 1913 by Indian emigrants in the US and Canada, mostly Punjabi, which tried to overthrow British rule through armed revolt.
Hindu-German Conspiracy
A joint plan of Indian revolutionaries and Germany during the First World War, which led to a long trial in San Francisco in 1917-18.

h: 'Joothi Gali': the country's dark present packed into one neighbourhood
dek: Poet Pawan Karan reviews Hrishikesh Sulabh's new novel, in which religion is a tool for property and dominance and every lane is slowly becoming a 'defiled lane'.
body: On The Wire Hindi, poet Pawan Karan has reviewed Hrishikesh Sulabh's novel 'Joothi Gali' (The Defiled Lane), which he sees as a sequel to Sulabh's previous novel 'Data Pir'. The story is about a lane where every family has some scheme: to increase its wealth, to save its property or to grab someone else's. Right in the middle of all these schemes sits religion.

According to the reviewer, religious hatred has turned every lane in the country into a 'defiled lane', and rich colonies and tall apartment blocks are no different: the same forced donations, huge pandals (festival tents), DJs and some man who has made himself the contractor of religion.

At the centre of the story is Bambam Bhaiya, leader of the 'Veer Hanuman Dal', the biggest product of this climate. Using a crack in the Hanuman idol as an excuse, he takes over the temple, the priest and a nearby shop are thrown out, and later one of his associates opens a shop for puja items right there. Some students from the lane are taken away by men posing as police or terrorists, who think they are Muslims; who these men were and what happened to the students, the novel leaves to the reader.

Pawan Karan praises Sulabh's fine, realistic portrayal, and also the way he handles a serious subject with light satire and does not add fuel to the communal fire. He finds memorable Janakdulari, who answers Bambam Bhaiya sharply, and Babbo, who forms a band of girls of her own.

The criticism is clear too. According to the reviewer, several women are defined only by the men around them and by old moulds, the characters are so crowded that the next one arrives before any one picture becomes clear, and the novel shows no organised resistance to the abuse of power. Even so, he sees the almost inevitable path to justice crafted for the lane's injustice as proof of the writer's skill.
nazar: Through the novel, this review puts a finger on the changed face of our neighbourhoods: religion is now less faith and more a business of grabbing and earning, and its contractor is the new ruler of the lane.
In our view the reviewer's question about the absence of resistance is the most important. If literature only maps the darkness and does not see those who fight it, it tells only half the truth.
sawal: Who made someone the contractor of religion in your lane?
ref: Hrishikesh Sulabh
Hindi fiction writer and playwright; according to the review, 'Joothi Gali' comes after his novel 'Data Pir'.
Data Pir
Hrishikesh Sulabh's previous novel, which the reviewer sees as the background to 'Joothi Gali'.
